newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Poverty, drugs, free trade on Kohl's Latin agenda.
newsitem.headline: Poverty, drugs, free trade on Kohl's Latin agenda.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl called on Sunday for closer international cooperation to fight unemployment, poverty and drugs and praised Latin American moves towards free trade.

"Nowadays no single nation in the world can face alone these challenges," he said at the start of a three-day visit to Argentina, the first leg of a week-long Latin American tour that also includes Brazil and Mexico.

At a ceremony commemorating the 100th anniversary of the foundation of the Goethe German school in Buenos Aires, Kohl said he was happy to be able to count "our good and loyal friends in Argentina" among those who are facing the challenges.
Kohl arrived late on Saturday and was meeting on Sunday with leaders of the German-Argentine community. On Monday he is scheduled to meet with President Carlos Menem and visit a Mercedes Benz plant.
The chancellor, who was accompanied by scores of German businessmen, hailed Argentina's moves towards regional ecomomic integration.
Argentina has formed with Brazil, Uruguay and Paraguay, the Mercosur customs union, a free-trade bloc that recently incorporated Chile and is now attracting other Latin American nations.
"Argentina's ... good neighbour policy and its efforts to promote regional cooperation and integration deserve praise and respect," Kohl said.
The German leader touched a sensitive chord when he made a passing mention of German Jews attending the ceremony.

Argentina is home to one of the world's largest Jewish communities and also has been a safe haven for notorious Nazi war criminals, including Holocaust architect Adolf Eichmann and SS Captain Erich Priebke.

Eichmann was abducted by Israeli commandos in 1960 and taken to Israel where he was tried and executed. Priebke was recently extradited to Rome to face trial for Italy's worst Second World War war crime -- the Ardeatine Caves massacre.

The daily Clarin on Sunday printed an interview with Ruben Beraja, Argentine Jewish community leader and vice president of the World Jewish Congress, in which he said he suspected part of the gold the Nazis stole from Jews may have ended up in Argentina.

"Funds may have been brought from Germany to South American countries," Beraja said. "Argentina may have been one of them. I have been informed that there are elements in U.S. archives pointing to a main route, which could be Argentina."
On Tuesday, Kohl is due to fly to Brasilia for talks with President Fernando Henrique Cardoso and to meet members of Congress and business representatives.

The German leader will then go to Mexico to meet President Ernesto Zedillo on Thursday. He is also set to address the Senate, meet Mexican trade and industry representatives and visit a Volkswagen plant.
This is the chancellor's second visit to Argentina and third to Mexico and Brazil. Kohl is scheduled to return to Germany on Sept. 21.
